title: The Growing Square Mystery
outcome: The student will explain why doubling the sides of a square quadruples its area because growth happens in two dimensions simultaneously.
subject: math

concepts.title: The Growing Square Mystery
concepts.centralCause: When both dimensions of a flat shape are multiplied by a factor k, the area increases by k squared because the shape grows in both length and width at once.
conditions: Both dimensions (length and width) must be scaled by the same factor
The thickness or coverage per unit remains constant

cards.title: Counting the Squares

fact.statement: Area is the number of unit squares needed to cover a shape's surface.
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids

hook.question: If you have a 3x3 square made of 9 tiles, what happens if you double the length of every side?
hook.predictPrompt: How many tiles do you think the new square needs? Guess, and say why.

cards.explanation: Area measures the surface space inside a boundary. Think of a square as a grid. A 3x3 square uses 9 small squares. When you double the sides to 6x6, you aren't just adding a row; you are adding rows and columns simultaneously. This creates a much larger space than just doubling the original count.

action.instruction: Take 9 sticky notes and arrange them in a 3x3 square. Imagine doubling the side length to 6. Predict how many notes you'd need to fill the new 6x6 area, then count how many fit in a 6x6 grid.

worlds.scene: A wizard is enchanting a magic tile. He needs to know how many tiles cover the floor of a square room.
worlds.illustration: A grid of 9 squares forming a large square.

question.prompt: If you have a square garden that is 2 meters wide and 2 meters long, and you decide to make it 4 meters wide and 4 meters long, how much more space will you have for plants?

key.expectedCause: The area becomes 4 times larger because both the width and the length doubled.
acceptable: It becomes 16 square meters because 4 times 4 is 16
key.typicalMistake: The area will double because the sides doubled.
key.followUp: Why doesn't doubling the sides only double the area?

criteria.example: Because both the width and length are doubling, the total space grows in two directions at once.

cards.title: The Two-Way Growth

fact.statement: Scaling a square's sides by a factor of k multiplies the area by k squared.
conditions: Both sides scaled by the same factor
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids

hook.question: Why does a 6x6 square hold four times as much as a 3x3 square?
hook.predictPrompt: What if every side gets three times longer? Guess how many times bigger the area gets, and say why.

cards.explanation: When you scale a square, you are stretching it in two directions: length and width. If you triple the sides, the length becomes 3 times longer AND the width becomes 3 times wider. The total area grows by 3 times 3, which is 9. This is why scaling is not a simple 1-to-1 increase.

action.instruction: Imagine a 3x3 square. In your mind, triple the side length to 9. Predict how many times larger the area becomes compared to the original 3x3, then think about how many 3x3 squares fit into a 9x9 square.

worlds.scene: A dragon's hoard grows. A square gold coin is replaced by a square that is 3 times wider.
worlds.illustration: A 3x3 grid showing how 9 small squares fit into a 9x9 grid.

question.prompt: If you have a square piece of paper and you triple the length of each side, how many times larger will the area of the paper become? Why?

key.expectedCause: It becomes 9 times larger because both the length and width are tripled (3 times 3).
acceptable: The area is 9 times larger because it grows in two directions.
key.typicalMistake: It will be 3 times larger because the sides are 3 times longer.
key.followUp: What would happen if we only tripled the length but kept the width the same?

criteria.example: It becomes 9 times larger because both dimensions are multiplied by 3.

cards.title: The Rectangle Exception

fact.statement: If only one side of a rectangle is doubled, the area only doubles.
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids

hook.question: What happens if you double the length of a rectangle but keep the width exactly the same?
hook.predictPrompt: Only the length gets twice as long, the width stays the same. How much bigger does the area get? Guess, and say why.

cards.explanation: Area is length times width. If you only change one dimension, like the length, the width stays constant. Therefore, the area only grows by that single change. This is different from a square where both sides change at once. To double the area of a rectangle, you only need to double one side.

action.instruction: Imagine a rectangle that is 2 units wide and 3 units long. Imagine doubling only the length to 6 units while keeping the width at 2. Predict the new area, then calculate it.

worlds.scene: A wizard's scroll is stretched. He makes it twice as long but it stays the same width.

question.prompt: A rug is 2 m by 3 m. A new rug is 2 m by 6 m. How did the floor it covers change, and why?

key.expectedCause: The area doubled because only one dimension (length) was changed while the other stayed the same.
acceptable: It doubled because only the length was doubled.
key.typicalMistake: It quadrupled because the length was doubled.
key.followUp: How would the area change if we doubled both the length and the width?

cards.title: Paint vs. Fences

fact.statement: Flat surfaces (paint, tiles) scale with area, while edges (fences, frames) scale with perimeter.
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids

hook.question: You make a square garden with every side twice as long. Do you need more fence or more grass seed — and how much more of each?
hook.predictPrompt: Guess how much more fence and how much more grass seed the bigger garden needs, and say why.

cards.explanation: Perimeter is the distance around the outside (a line). Area is the space inside (a surface). When you double the sides of a square, the perimeter (the fence) only doubles because it's a 1D measurement. However, the area (the grass) quadruples because it grows in two directions. Paint and tiles also follow the area rule.

action.instruction: Imagine a square garden with a fence around it. If you double the side length, predict if the fence length doubles or quadruples. Then, think about the grass inside.

worlds.scene: A knight builds a fence around a square castle. The castle grows in size.
worlds.illustration: A square with a border (fence) and a filled interior (grass).

question.prompt: You make a square picture with every side twice as long. How much longer is its frame, and how much more paint does the picture need? Why?

key.expectedCause: The frame goes around the edge, so it only gets 2 times longer; the paint covers the whole surface, which grows in length and width at once, so it needs 4 times as much.
acceptable: Frame is the perimeter and doubles, paint is the area and becomes 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger.
key.typicalMistake: Both double, because the sides doubled.
key.followUp: How many copies of the old picture fit into the new one?

criteria.example: The fence is a perimeter and only grows in one direction, while the grass covers the area which grows in two directions.

cards.title: The Master Architect

fact.statement: Scaling a 2D shape by factor k results in an area multiplied by k squared.
conditions: Both sides scaled by the same factor
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, section 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-4-use-properties-of-rectangles-triangles-and-trapezoids

hook.question: You are an architect designing a square plaza. If you want to make the plaza 5 times wider and 5 times longer, how many times larger will the area be?
hook.predictPrompt: If the plaza gets 5 times wider and 5 times longer, how many times more stone tiles will it need? Guess, and say why.

cards.explanation: Since the plaza is a flat shape, when you multiply both the length and the width by 5, the area grows by 5 times 5. This is because the growth happens in both directions simultaneously. The area is always the product of the two sides. If both sides are multiplied by 5, the total area is multiplied by 25.

action.instruction: Imagine a square plaza. If you multiply both sides by 5, predict how many times the area increases. Then, calculate the area of a 1x1 square and a 5x5 square to verify.

worlds.scene: An architect designs a square plaza for a royal palace.

question.prompt: A square photo is printed as a poster with every side 10 times longer. How many times more paper does the poster need? Why?

acceptable: 10 rows of 10 photos fit into the poster, so it is 100 photos big.
key.typicalMistake: 10 times more, because the sides are 10 times longer.
key.followUp: How many small photos fit along one side of the poster, and how many rows are there?

criteria.example: It becomes 25 times larger because both the length and width were multiplied by 5.
